item.content:encoded:
India already has its first space-tech unicorn. Skyroot Aerospace crossed the $1 billion valuation mark in May 2026 and, two months later, its Vikram-1 became the first privately developed Indian rocket to reach orbit. Those milestones confirm that India's private space ecosystem has moved well beyond aspiration. 

The more interesting question is what happens next and whether we are looking in the right places for it. 

India's opportunity in space is not limited to producing another rocket company. It lies in building an entire space economy: the infrastructure, components, manufacturing systems, robotics, software and services that will make space progressively more accessible, industrial and ultimately habitable. 

That economy will not appear in one leap. It will be built in layers. 

The first layer is cheaper, more repeatable access to orbit. Reusable launch systems and a growing private launch market can gradually turn space travel from an exceptional event into an economic activity. Once access becomes more reliable, the next layer is orbital infrastructure consisting of more capable stations, platforms, communications networks and servicing systems. 

Infrastructure then creates the conditions for industry. Manufacturing and fuelling can move into orbit. The vacuum and microgravity environment may enable forms of precision manufacturing that are difficult to reproduce on Earth, while in-space resources could eventually reduce the need to lift every material from the ground. Components, fuel and equipment will have to move through a supply chain that extends beyond Earth. 

Robots will be the first workforce in that economy. They will construct, maintain and operate facilities in conditions where a permanent human presence is still impractical. Over time, closed environments may begin producing plants and food, initially managed largely by autonomous systems. Once infrastructure, industry and life-support systems have been demonstrated at increasing levels of complexity, sustained animal and eventually human habitation will become a reality. Cheap transport, then infrastructure, then industry and after that robotics and life-support. That is the long arc through which humans become a genuinely interplanetary species. Each stage creates the market and technical requirements for the next. 

Seen this way, the next major Indian space company may not be building a rocket at all. It may be developing propulsion, power systems, sensors, communications, navigation, orbital robotics, satellite servicing, space situational awareness, Earth-observation tools, advanced materials, in-space manufacturing or the data applications built on top of them. Some of these businesses may not even describe themselves as space companies today.

India's own ambitions reflect the scale of this opportunity. The government estimates that the domestic space economy could grow from about $8.4 billion in 2022 to $44 billion by 2033, including $11 billion in exports. That cannot be delivered by a handful of headline companies. It will require hundreds of specialised businesses building different layers of the system. 

Around 440 space-technology startups are registered on the government's Startup India portal. Separately, Tracxn covers 285 space-tech companies, which have raised roughly $871 million across 241 funding rounds. Only 72 of those companies have received institutional equity funding, and more than 60% of the capital has gone to the ten most-funded startups. The two datasets use different definitions, but they point to the same reality that entrepreneurial activity is expanding much faster than institutional capital is reaching it. 

The government has begun responding to this gap with a much broader capital and infrastructure architecture. The Rs.1,000 crore IN-SPACe venture fund has been operationalised with SIDBI Venture Capital. IN-SPACe has also launched a Rs 500-crore Technology Adoption Fund, seed and pre-incubation programmes, shared technical facilities, a Satellite Bus as a Service initiative, access to ISRO infrastructure and technology-transfer pathways. By July 2026, 118 technology-transfer agreements covering 83 ISRO and Department of Space technologies had been signed with Indian industry. 

The support extends beyond space. The Rs 1 lakh-crore Research, Development and Innovation Scheme is designed to provide long-term, low-cost financing for indigenous technologies at Technology Readiness Level 4 and above. Startup India Fund of Funds 2.0 adds another Rs 10,000 crore, with specific windows for deep-tech funds, micro-VCs and technology-led manufacturing.These are important signals that policy is going full throttle in recognising that frontier technologies require different timelines, instruments and a willingness to back them at scale. 

The remaining challenge is not whether India is doing enough in absolute terms. It is whether the different parts of this architecture connect early enough to the founders and technologies from which the next layer of the space economy will emerge. Series A cheque is meaningful for a company ready to scale. It does not solve the problem faced by a two-person team in a university lab still trying to establish whether a thruster design works outside a simulation.

This is the structural challenge in financing deep tech. Conventional venture capital operates against a defined fund life and looks for commercial traction within a relatively compressed period. Deep-tech companies often cannot work to that clock. They may need years of research, specialised infrastructure, testing and certification before they can address a meaningful commercial market. 

Patient capital is sometimes mistaken for capital without discipline. It is the opposite: capital that applies the right discipline to the right stage. The milestones simply come in a different order - proof of science, prototype, reliability, certification, first customer and then scale. The journey from technical proof to meaningful revenue is often measured in years, not months. That makes patient capital not just useful, but essential. It also means we need to rethink where the journey begins, including the role universities and campuses can play in creating the science, talent and early-stage companies that frontier industries will ultimately depend on. 

This is where campuses matter. 

Campus Fund has spent the past several years tracking and investing in student entrepreneurship in India, and the shift has been hard to miss. More than 7,300 startups entered the Campus Fund funnel in 2025, while DeepTech became its largest category at nearly 17% (compared to 8.4% in 2024) and the nature of the founders is changing too. The number of PhD founders in the funnel rose from just 35 in 2020-21 to 237 in 2024-25, almost a sevenfold increase. Edtech startups built around coaching and content are down 36% and traditional services startups are down 52%. Students are visibly choosing harder, more defensible problems over easier ones. 

This matters because many of the technologies that will define the next decade are being worked on not in corporate strategy rooms, but in university labs by students and researchers spending years on narrow, unglamorous problems. They often have access to professors, laboratories, equipment and technically fluent peers. What they lack is institutional credibility and an early source of risk capital. 

A student with a working prototype may struggle to raise a first cheque. The same founder, a few years later, with a company, customers and external validation, may find it much easier to raise several crores. The first institutional cheque should follow technical insight and evidence that something is possible. 

None of this works if we pretend early-stage deep tech is a safe bet because it isn't and it was never going to be. Some of these propulsion systems won't fire. Some sensors will work beautifully in a lab and prove impossible to manufacture at cost. Some technologies will be ready only to find that the market has shifted or a competing technology has emerged. Others will simply be overtaken by better technology. That is the nature of frontier technology. 

But if capital arrives only after product-market fit has been established, we risk filtering out precisely the technologies that need time and early backing to reveal their potential. A small pre-seed cheque to a student team is not only a startup investment. It helps keep research alive inside the university system and gives founders the option to build a company around work that might otherwise remain in a laboratory. 

The first Indian space unicorn is no longer a prediction. The harder question is whether we can find the next one before the rest of the world knows its name. It may not be sitting in a boardroom. It may still be in a hostel room, where two founders are arguing at 2 a.m. about whether the prototype can actually work.

-- Richa Bajpai, Founder and CEO at Campus Fund

item.title: Why AI-powered intelligence is every winning brand’s secret sauce
item.description: As AI reshapes ecommerce, brands are shifting focus from customer acquisition to intelligent fulfilment, inventory management and customer experience. The article explores how AI and agentic systems enable smarter, faster operational decisions.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the playbook for building a winning consumer brand was simple: a compelling product, a strong brand identity, and smart customer acquisition. Those fundamentals still hold, but they no longer decide who wins.

Today's battle is fought in fragments of attention, where brands have seconds to convert interest into a purchase. And the moment “Buy Now” is clicked, a second, harder battle begins: fast fulfilment, a seamless delivery experience, and effortless handling of queries and returns - the moments that actually earn loyalty.

Amid endless channels and ever-shifting marketing strategies, the real differentiator has moved downstream: it's the intelligence behind every operational decision made after the click.

Artificial intelligence is rapidly becoming this intelligence layer. No longer limited to chatbots or content generation, AI is transforming how brands forecast demand, allocate inventory, orchestrate fulfilment, engage customers, and optimise operations in real time.

This shift comes at a time when commerce itself has grown far more complex. Consumers now discover, evaluate, and buy across a maze of touchpoints - brand websites, marketplaces, quick commerce, social commerce, and physical stores - often within a single purchase journey. Powering every one of those purchases is a complex web of inventory nodes, warehouses, logistics partners, and engagement systems that must move in perfect synchronisation.

For brands, this translates into a flood of operational data. Every inventory movement, customer interaction, order update, warehouse scan, and delivery milestone becomes a signal that can influence the next business decision. What begins as a simple online business quickly turns into a web of real-time, interconnected decisions - each one shaping the customer experience.

Until a few years ago, brands and marketplaces operated on Systems of Record - a single source of operational truth that captured transactions and helped manage inventory. Ecommerce enablement SaaS platforms turned these Systems of Insight - real-time dashboards and analytics that let businesses move from reactive to data-driven decision-making.

The next phase of this evolution is now underway. Building on this rich data and technology-enabled processes, these Systems of Record and Insight are becoming Systems of Intelligence - where AI is not just analysing information, but actively framing recommendations and executing decisions across business operations.

Consider a fashion retailer during a festive sale. Thousands of orders may arrive simultaneously across its website, marketplaces, and quick commerce platforms. Instead of relying on manual rules or static workflows, AI can continuously evaluate inventory availability, warehouse capacity, delivery timelines, shipping costs, and customer location before automatically routing each order through the most efficient fulfilment path. It can also spot that a fast-moving product is about to run out in one city while stock sits healthy elsewhere and line up a transfer before availability ever becomes the customer's problem.

This matters even more in an omnichannel world, where customers expect availability wherever and however they shop. Delivering on that promise takes more than inventory visibility - it demands continuous coordination across allocation, order orchestration, warehouse operations, logistics, and customer communication. AI makes that coordination possible at a scale and speed manual decision-making simply can't match.

The next frontier here is Agentic AI. Unlike traditional automation, which follows predefined workflows, Agentic AI can reason across multiple variables, recommend the next best course of action, and autonomously execute routine operational decisions within business-defined guardrails. Whether prioritising high-value orders during peak demand, responding to supply chain disruptions, or flagging fulfilment bottlenecks before they bite, these systems move beyond supporting human decisions to actively driving them.

This marks a fundamental shift in how brands approach growth. Acquiring customers remains critical, but sustainable growth increasingly depends on what happens after demand is generated. Rather than adding operational headcount every time order volumes spike, businesses are investing in intelligent platforms that let them scale without proportionately scaling complexity. The goal is no longer simply to process more orders - it's to make better operational decisions, faster and more consistently.

Ecommerce enablement platforms, with deep data and operational ties into brands, are already building this future. AI-first SaaS tools are no longer just software - they're becoming operational partners, continuously improving how the business runs.

Tomorrow's market leaders won't necessarily be the brands with the biggest marketing budgets. They'll be the brands whose technology lets them operate smarter, adapt faster, and make better decisions every single day. Their competitive advantage will increasingly come from the intelligence behind every business decision they make.

(Kapil Makhija is the MD & CEO of Unicommerce eSolutions Limited)

item.title: GIVA raises $100M in Multiples-led round; India’s Rs 3 lakh Cr data centre buildout

item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader,

India’s data centre industry is poised for a five-fold expansion, with installed capacity expected to reach 7.5 GW by March 2030, attracting investments of more than Rs 3 lakh crore over the next four financial years, according to Crisil Ratings. Demand from generative AI, cloud adoption and enterprise digitalisation is driving the build-out. However, power connectivity, regulatory clearances and project execution will be crucial to keeping projects on track. 

In other news, Bengaluru-based jewellery brand GIVA has raised $100 million in a funding round led by Multiples Alternate Asset Management. The company plans to use the capital to strengthen its leadership team, expand manufacturing and deepen its offline presence. It currently operates more than 400 stores across India and Sri Lanka, selling silver, gold and lab-grown diamond jewellery. 

Meanwhile, Google has launched Dreambeans, an experimental AI-powered app in India that turns activity across selected services, including Gmail, Calendar, Gemini, Photos, Search and YouTube into personalised stories. Available to users aged 18 and above on Android and iOS, it supports 14 Indian languages. 

In the drone sector, ideaForge returned to profitability in Q2 FY27, reporting revenue of Rs 91.3 crore, up 124% year-on-year, and a profit after tax of Rs 6.5 crore, against a loss of Rs 19.6 crore a year earlier. Its EBITDA stood at Rs 23.2 crore. 

Yet progress in business remains uneven. Women hold 30.5% of management positions worldwide, according to an International Labour Organization survey covering companies in 99 countries. Their share has risen only gradually over three decades, despite gains in education, highlighting barriers to career advancement and unequal care responsibilities.

News

Apple hits record India revenue in September quarter

Apple posted its strongest-ever September quarter revenue in India, with the country emerging as a key growth market amid robust demand for its devices. The performance was driven by record iPhone upgrades and Mac sales, alongside the launch of Apple Pay in India. Globally, the tech giant reported quarterly revenue of $114.48 billion, even as rising memory costs and supply constraints weighed on operations. 

Key takeaways: 

  • Apple reported its highest-ever September quarter revenue in India, driven by record iPhone upgrades and strong MacBook demand. 
  • Quarterly revenue rose 11.72% year-on-year to $114.48 billion, while FY26 revenue increased 15.06% to a record $478.83 billion.
  • Higher memory prices, advanced chip supply constraints and increased operating expenses put pressure on margins, despite strong iPhone and Services performance.

Funding

VC funding into Indian startups plunges 66% in October 

Venture capital funding into Indian startups fell sharply in October, dropping 66% year-on-year to $581 million, according to YourStory Research. The decline was largely driven by the absence of large-value funding rounds, with Even Healthcare's $50 million raise emerging as the month's biggest deal. Despite the subdued month, startups raised $10.4 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, putting the ecosystem on track to match or exceed its 2025 funding total.

item.title: 5 lessons from the book Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan
item.description: Discover five lessons from Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan about storytelling, content marketing, community building, PR, and social media.
item.content:encoded:
Super Cool Startup: Get Your Early-Stage Marketing Right for the AI Age by Sairam Krishnan is a practical guide for entrepreneurs, startup founders, and marketers who want to build brands that people recognise, trust, and remember.

Drawing on his experience working with companies such as Freshworks and Atomicwork, and his work in the startup ecosystem, Krishnan explains why having a great product is not enough to build a successful business.

Startups also need a clear story, meaningful content, an engaged community, effective public relations, and a strong social media presence.

The book focuses on five fundamental pillars of early-stage marketing: storytelling, content, community, PR and guerrilla marketing, and social media. It offers useful insights into how businesses can earn attention and build a marketing engine, particularly in an era when AI has made content creation easier but strategic judgement more important.

5 Important lessons from Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan

1. A great product needs a great story

One of the biggest lessons from Super Cool Startup is that building a good product is only one part of building a successful business. People also need to understand why the product exists and why they should care about it.

A startup may have an innovative product, talented founders, and a promising business model. However, if it cannot communicate its purpose and value clearly, it may struggle to attract customers and stand out in a competitive market.

Krishnan emphasises storytelling as the foundation of startup marketing. A compelling brand story explains the problem a company wants to solve, the people it wants to help, and what makes its approach different.

For example, instead of simply describing a product through its features, a startup can explain the everyday problem it solves and how it makes customers' lives easier.

The lesson: Do not just tell people what your product does. Give them a reason to care about it. A clear and relatable story can help a startup build recognition, trust, and a stronger connection with its audience.

2. Content is how you build trust

A strong brand story needs the right content to reach its audience. This is where content marketing becomes important.

The book highlights content as one of the essential pillars of early-stage marketing. Whether it is an article, newsletter, case study, video, or social media post, content allows businesses to communicate their ideas and demonstrate their expertise.

However, creating content simply to remain active online is not enough. Businesses need to understand what their target audience wants to learn, what problems they are trying to solve, and what information would genuinely help them.

For instance, a startup offering marketing software could publish practical guides, industry insights, customer stories, and educational videos instead of constantly promoting its product.

This approach helps potential customers understand the brand before they even consider making a purchase.

The lesson: Focus on creating useful content rather than producing content just for visibility. When businesses consistently offer valuable information, they have a better opportunity to build credibility and earn their audience's trust.

3. Build a community, not just a customer base

Another important lesson from Super Cool Startup is that successful brands should focus on building communities around their products and ideas.

Customers may purchase a product because they need it, but a community gives them a reason to stay connected with the brand. When people feel involved in a company's journey, they can become supporters who recommend its products, share their experiences, and introduce others to the business.

Krishnan identifies community-building as a fundamental part of early-stage marketing. Instead of treating customers as people who simply purchase products, startups should create opportunities for meaningful interactions.

This could include organising online discussions, hosting webinars, creating customer groups, encouraging feedback, or bringing together people with similar interests.

For example, a fitness startup could build a community where members share their progress, exchange advice, participate in challenges, and support one another.

Such interactions can help businesses develop stronger relationships with their audiences.

The lesson: Do not focus only on acquiring customers. Give people a reason to become part of your brand's journey. A supportive community can become one of a startup's most valuable long-term assets.

4. You do not always need a huge budget to get attention

Startups often operate with limited resources, which makes traditional advertising and large marketing campaigns difficult to afford. However, getting noticed does not always require spending a significant amount of money.

In Super Cool Startup, Krishnan highlights public relations (PR) and guerrilla marketing as important ways to generate attention and make a brand more recognisable.

Public relations helps businesses build credibility through media coverage, industry conversations, founder interviews, and meaningful announcements. Guerrilla marketing, meanwhile, involves creative and unconventional approaches to reaching people.

A startup can use these methods to create memorable experiences and generate conversations without depending entirely on expensive advertising campaigns.

For instance, a small business could organise an interesting public activation, collaborate with a relevant creator, or develop a creative campaign that encourages people to share it organically.

The key is to understand what makes an idea interesting enough for people to talk about.

The lesson: Creativity and strategic thinking can sometimes achieve what a large advertising budget cannot. Focus on developing memorable ideas that give people a reason to notice and discuss your brand.

5. Use social media to make your story travel

Having a great product, an interesting brand story, and valuable content means little if the right audience never discovers them. This is why social media plays an important role in a startup's marketing strategy.

Krishnan identifies social media as the fifth pillar of building a super-cool startup. It provides businesses with platforms to distribute their stories, communicate with customers, showcase their products, and participate in conversations relevant to their industries.

However, effective social media marketing involves more than regularly uploading posts. Businesses need to understand which platforms their audiences use, what type of content they engage with, and how to communicate in a way that feels relevant.

For example, a B2B startup might use LinkedIn to share industry insights, founder perspectives, and customer success stories, while a consumer brand could use Instagram to showcase products, collaborate with creators, and build an engaged audience.

The important thing is to ensure that social media supports the larger marketing strategy rather than becoming an isolated activity.

The lesson: Treat social media as a distribution channel for your brand story. Use it strategically to reach the right people, build relationships, and make your business more recognisable.

Final thoughts

Super Cool Startup by Sairam Krishnan offers practical insights into entrepreneurship, branding, and modern marketing. It shows why a strong product needs effective storytelling, clear positioning, and meaningful audience connections to succeed.

The five lessons explore how storytelling, content, community-building, PR, and social media shape a startup's marketing strategy. The book also highlights that while AI makes content creation easier, good marketing still relies on human judgement and an understanding of audience needs.

Whether you are a founder or marketer, the book offers useful ideas for building a brand people understand, trust, and want to talk about.

item.title: 5 Books you must add to your November 2026 reading list
item.description: Discover five books to add to your November 2026 reading list, from emotional literary fiction and romantic suspense to thought-provoking dystopian novels.
item.content:encoded:
November is a wonderful time to discover new authors, explore different genres, and make room for stories that offer fresh perspectives.

Whether you enjoy emotional literary fiction, psychological suspense, thought-provoking dystopian novels, or stories about love and ambition, the right book can make your reading month memorable.

If you are planning your November 2026 reading list, these five books deserve your attention. Each offers a different reading experience, from complicated relationships and personal struggles to questions about technology, identity, and human connection.

5 Books worth adding to your reading list this November

1. The Correspondent by Virginia Evans

If you enjoy character-driven stories that explore relationships, memories, and the importance of communication, The Correspondent by Virginia Evans is an excellent choice.

The novel follows Sybil Van Antwerp, a retired lawyer who communicates with the people in her life through letters. Through her correspondence with family members, friends, and strangers, readers gradually discover her personality, complicated relationships, regrets, and experiences.

What makes the novel particularly interesting is its epistolary format. Instead of following a conventional narrative, the story unfolds through letters, allowing readers to understand the characters through their words and interactions.

The book explores ageing, forgiveness, grief, family connections, and the ways people make sense of their past.

Why should you read it?

If you enjoy emotionally layered stories that make you reflect on relationships and the things left unsaid, this book deserves a place on your November reading list. It is also a refreshing choice for readers who want to explore a storytelling format different from traditional novels.

2. Broken Country by Clare Leslie Hall

For readers who enjoy emotional storytelling combined with romance, family drama, and suspense, Broken Country by Clare Leslie Hall is a compelling choice.

The novel follows Beth, a woman living in the English countryside whose seemingly settled life is disrupted when Gabriel Wolfe, a man from her past, returns to her village with his young son.

His arrival brings back memories, unresolved feelings, and questions about the choices Beth made years earlier. As the story develops, a tragic incident changes everything and forces the characters to confront the consequences of their decisions.

One of the book's strongest elements is its exploration of love, loyalty, grief, and the complicated relationship between the past and the present.

Why should you read it?

If you enjoy emotionally intense stories with unexpected revelations, complicated relationships, and a touch of mystery, Broken Country is worth picking up. It is particularly suited to readers who love stories that keep them invested until the final pages.

3. The Dream Hotel by Laila Lalami

If you enjoy dystopian fiction that makes you question the future of technology and society, The Dream Hotel by Laila Lalami deserves a place on your reading list.

The novel imagines a world where technology has advanced to the point that people's dreams can be monitored and analysed. The story follows Sara, a woman whose private dreams become the basis for an algorithm's assessment of her potential risk to society.

As she finds herself caught in a system that questions her freedom and autonomy, the novel explores the frightening consequences of allowing technology to influence deeply personal aspects of human life.

Through its unsettling premise, Lalami raises important questions about privacy, surveillance, artificial intelligence, and the growing influence of algorithms on everyday decisions.

Why should you read it?

This book is an excellent choice for readers who enjoy speculative fiction with real-world relevance. If you are interested in technology, artificial intelligence, and questions about personal freedom, The Dream Hotel will give you plenty to think about.

4. Atmosphere by Taylor Jenkins Reid

Taylor Jenkins Reid is known for writing emotionally engaging novels with memorable characters, and Atmosphere is another compelling addition to her bibliography.

Set in the 1980s, the novel follows Joan Goodwin, an astronomy professor who joins NASA's space shuttle programme after pursuing an opportunity she has always dreamed about.

As Joan enters the demanding world of astronaut training, she encounters professional challenges, new relationships, and experiences that change how she understands ambition and love.

The novel explores the sacrifices involved in pursuing extraordinary dreams while examining the emotional connections that make life meaningful. It also highlights the experiences of women working in a field where they have historically been underrepresented.

Why should you read it?

If you enjoy stories about ambitious women, unexpected relationships, and the courage to pursue your dreams, Atmosphere is a wonderful choice. It combines the excitement of space exploration with an emotional story about identity, ambition, and love.

5. The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai

For readers who appreciate literary fiction that explores identity, family, culture, and belonging, The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny by Kiran Desai is a book worth considering.

The novel follows Sonia and Sunny, two young Indians whose lives unfold across different countries and cultures. As their paths intersect, the story explores their experiences with family expectations, relationships, migration, and the search for personal identity.

Through its characters, Desai examines the complicated relationship between individual ambitions and the expectations inherited from family and society.

The novel also explores loneliness and the desire to find a place where we feel understood. It raises questions about how our cultural backgrounds, relationships, and experiences influence the people we eventually become.

Why should you read it?

If you enjoy immersive literary fiction with complex characters and meaningful observations about society, this book deserves your attention. It is particularly appealing to readers interested in stories about belonging, cultural identity, and the complexities of human relationships.

Final thoughts

A good reading list should include stories that entertain you, challenge your thinking, and introduce you to perspectives you might not have considered before.

These five books offer something different for November 2026. The Correspondent explores relationships through letters, Broken Country combines romance with suspense, and The Dream Hotel examines the consequences of technological surveillance. Meanwhile, Atmosphere celebrates ambition and human connection, while The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny explores identity, family, and belonging.

You do not necessarily have to read all five books in one month. Pick the one that matches your current reading mood, make time for a few pages every day, and enjoy discovering a new story.

Sometimes, the best way to end a month is with a book that leaves you thinking long after you have turned its final page.

item.title: VC funding into Indian startups plunges 66% in October
item.description: The steep drop in venture capital funding into Indian startups has been primarily due to near absence of large value deals in the month of October.
item.content:encoded:
Venture capital (VC) funding into Indian startups touched a new low in October, with a decline of 66% against October of last year.

When compared with the VC funding raised in September 2025, the drop was 49%.

The total VC funding in October came in at just $581 million as compared with $1.6 billion in October 2025, according to YourStory Research. In the month of September 2026, the funding amount was $1.1 billion.

October saw 107 VC deals. In contrast, the September month saw 100 deals but the amount was higher. The same was the case in October 2025, where the number of deals was 99.

This steep drop in VC funding in October was primarily due to the complete absence of large value deals for the entire period. The highest funded deal for the month was from Even Healthcare at $50 million.

The last such decline was seen in May when the total reached $651 million.

These developments highlight the challenges faced by the startup ecosystem while raising capital. Global investors, particularly in the US, are pouring capital into AI, while India still lacks a significant number of viable AI startups.

Few AI firms in India that have managed to pull funding include Sarvam, Emergent or Neysa. This shows India has a long way to go to establish AI startups that gain investor interest.

Through the first 10 months of 2026, Indian startups raised $10.4 billion, putting the ecosystem on pace to match or surpass the $12 billion total recorded in 2025.

This low funding momentum was also reflected in the stage wise funding category. The late-stage funding category which generally attracts the highest amount saw only $97 million raised for the month of October. The top category was from the growth stage (250 million) followed by the early stage ($221 million).

The dominant trend for the Indian startup ecosystem for the last three years has been the highest volume of activity in terms of number of deals has been in the early-stage funding category but this segment does not draw in large amounts of money.

In terms of the top three segments that raised capital in October, the top categories were D2C, healthtech and automotive. The AI segment just raised $42 million in the month.

The top three cities which received VC funding in October were the usual ones: Bengaluru, Delhi-NCR and Mumbai. By and large, these three metros have consistently garnered an overwhelming majority of funding flowing into Indian startups with an occasional occurrence some other metros like Chennai, Hyderabad or Pune making it to the top three.

Overall, it has not been a positive picture for the Indian startup ecosystem in terms of VC funding so far and the only hope is that the situation will turn out for the better next year.

Edited by Affirunisa Kankudti

item.title: How Anju turned a personal food experiment into a snack brand expanding to 41 retail stores
item.description: At 60, Anju Kalhan is scaling Bliss by Anju, a bootstrapped healthy snacks brand selling plant-based products across 41 stores.
item.content:encoded:
A 20-year corporate career, an events business and eight marathons may not seem like the usual starting points for a food entrepreneur.

But Anju Kalhan's journey to building a healthy snacking brand has taken an unconventional route.

A graduate in Business Economics from the University of Delhi, Anju spent two decades working in corporate and industry organisations.

She served as a Senior Economist at ASSOCHAM and Deputy Director at the Hotel Association of India, where she also worked with SSH Rehman, former Managing Director of ITC Hotels.

She eventually left her corporate career to start an events company, organising FICCI events and corporate workshops. Alongside her professional commitments, she pursued fitness, completed eight marathons and trained as a yoga professional and fitness coach.

But it was a personal health experience that eventually led her towards the food business.

Today, she is the founder of Bliss by Anju, a food brand making plant-based snacks without added oil, ghee, dairy or refined ingredients.

What began with experiments in her home kitchen has grown into an operation with an in-house manufacturing facility and a retail presence across 41 stores in India.

A personal journey sparks a business idea

Anju says she had lived with high blood pressure for nearly 30 years, along with severe migraines and sinusitis. Health complications within her family, including diabetes and high blood pressure among her parents, also made her reconsider their everyday food habits.

During the Covid-19 pandemic, she began exploring plant-based whole-food diets, learning from coaches and studying the role of food in health.

She gradually removed ghee, cooking oil and highly processed packaged foods from her kitchen. According to Anju, she noticed significant improvements in her blood pressure and migraines within 90 days. Her mother, who was over 80, also experienced improvements in her diabetes and blood pressure after changing her diet, she says.

The experience encouraged Anju to look beyond her household and examine what was available in the market.

She visited organic stores, large retail outlets and shops selling artisanal products to find snacks that aligned with her new food choices. However, she found that many products marketed as healthy still contained palm oil or other added oils.

This exposed a gap she wanted to address.

"The healthy food is not tasty, and the tasty food is not healthy," was how Anju described the problem she encountered.

She decided to create snacks that could offer both. Rather than depend on oil and ghee for flavour, she began experimenting with Indian spices, nuts and seeds.

The company's earlier journey began with home-kitchen experiments in 2018-19, followed by selling at farmers' markets in 2019-20. As her understanding of whole-food eating evolved, she reworked the product range in 2023-24 to remove ghee and added oils.

From kitchen experiments to an in-house factory

Building a food business without a background in professional cooking or bakery operations meant learning several things along the way.

Anju says she is neither a trained chef nor a nutritionist. Instead, she approached product development through research, experimentation and a willingness to learn.

The brand's philosophy is built around plant-based whole foods and familiar ingredients. Its range includes granolas made with nuts and seeds, cookies prepared using chickpea flour, sattu and almonds, biscotti, sweets and savoury snacks such as matthi.

One of its products, tangy dates, uses dates, spices and lemon, offering an alternative to conventional packaged aam papad.

For Anju, spices are central to making the products flavourful without added fats. Cinnamon, cardamom and nutmeg, she explains, can bring aroma and flavour to snacks without relying on oil or ghee.

The company also pays attention to how its ingredients are prepared. Anju says nuts and seeds are washed, soaked and dried before being used in its products.

What started in her kitchen has now moved into manufacturing. The company operates an in-house factory in Okhla industrial area, where it makes its products.

Its approach is to cover different snacking occasions throughout the day, from morning granola to cookies with tea, biscotti with coffee and savoury snacks in the evening.

Taking the brand to more consumers

Bliss by Anju has expanded its distribution to 41 stores across India and is also available on Amazon and Blinkit.

The company has entered its third year of operations in its current phase of growth, according to Anju. It remains bootstrapped, and she says she is looking for investment to support the next stage of the business.

Building awareness remains one of the challenges. As a relatively small brand, Anju says she cannot afford large celebrity endorsements or extensive marketing campaigns. She is looking to reach consumers by communicating the thinking behind the products and the ingredients used to make them.

The brand's products can also be relatively expensive because of their use of nuts, seeds and other whole-food ingredients. Anju believes consumers should understand food labels and make informed choices about what they eat.

Her efforts extend beyond selling packaged snacks.

Through her association with the SHARAN community, she participates in cooking demonstrations and classes that teach people how to prepare food without oil and ghee. Many of these sessions are free or offered at a nominal charge.

She is also careful about how she positions her products. Anju says the snacks are not intended to replace fresh meals. Instead, they are meant for people who need convenient options while travelling, working in offices or packing food for children.

At 60, Anju is building a food business around an idea that emerged from her own experiences. Having moved from a corporate career to entrepreneurship and then into food manufacturing, she is now looking for investment and opportunities to expand Bliss by Anju.

For women considering entrepreneurship, her advice is simple: pursue the idea, even when the circumstances are not perfect. As she puts it, one should not be afraid of taking the plunge. Something worthwhile can emerge from the effort.

item.title: Startup news and updates: Daily roundup (November 3, 2026)
item.description: YourStory presents the daily news roundup from the Indian startup ecosystem and beyond. Here's the roundup for Tuesday, November 03, 2026.
item.content:encoded:
India continues to remain an important growth market for Apple as startups continue to raise funding across cheque sizes. YourStory brings you this and other latest developments across sectors.

Featured stories

India shines in Apple’s record September quarter

India emerged as a stellar growth market for Apple in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, registering an all-time company revenue record in the country. “We also set September quarter revenue records in both developed and emerging markets, in addition to an all-time record in India,” Apple Chief Executive Officer John Ternus said. The performance in India was propelled by a September quarter record for iPhone upgraders, with Worldpanel survey data ranking iPhone among the top-selling smartphone models in the country.

Read more

VC funding into Indian startups plunges 66% in October

Venture capital (VC) funding into Indian startups touched a new low in October, with a decline of 66% against October of last year. When compared with the VC funding raised in September 2025, the drop was 49%. The total VC funding in October came in at just $581 million as compared with $1.6 billion in October 2025, according to YourStory Research. In September 2026, the funding amount was $1.1 billion.

Read more

Funding news

PowerUp Money raises $10M to expand AI-led wealth management

PowerUp Money, a wealthtech platform offering mutual fund advice and digital wealth management services, has raised $10 million in a funding round led by Flourish Ventures, an early-stage investment firm. Existing investors Peak XV Partners, Accel, Blume Ventures, Kae Capital, 8i Ventures and DeVC also participated.

The Bengaluru-based company plans to use a significant portion of the capital to develop its AI-powered wealth management platform and expand its managed advisory business.

Read more

Sachin Tendulkar backs Hitwicket maker Metasports Interactive

Metasports Interactive, the Hyderabad-based maker of cricket strategy game Hitwicket, has brought cricket legend Sachin Tendulkar on board as a strategic investor. He will also serve as the game’s brand ambassador.

The financial terms and valuation remain undisclosed. Existing backers include venture-capital firms Prime Venture Partners and Singapore’s Horizon Ventures, as well as cricket commentator Harsha Bhogle.

Read more

Upsurge India leads Rs 50 Cr secondary transaction in iD Fresh Food

Upsurge India has led a secondary transaction worth over Rs 50 crore in Bengaluru-based fresh-food brand iD Fresh Food, facilitating the exit of early investor Blue Ashva Capital. The transaction involved the transfer of approximately 1% equity in the company, with TG Fund and WW Ventures participating as co-leads.

Founded in 2005, iD Fresh specialises in preservative-free ready-to-cook products, including idli and dosa batter, Indian breads and chutneys. The company reported a revenue of over Rs 870 crore in FY26, compared with Rs 681 crore in FY25, representing growth of more than 25%. The transaction highlights growing institutional investor interest in established Indian consumer businesses and the increasing importance of secondary liquidity in private markets.

The Croffle Guys raises Rs 14 Cr in funding round led by V3 Ventures

Mumbai-based quick-service restaurant startup The Croffle Guys has raised Rs 14 crore in a funding round led by V3 Ventures, backed by Verlinvest, at a post-money valuation of Rs 100 crore. N.A.N. Partners also participated in the round. Founded in 2025, the company has expanded from two outlets to eight within a year and achieved an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 24 crore.

The startup plans to add more than 40 outlets, primarily across Mumbai and Delhi, with a selective presence in Pune. It is targeting an annualised revenue run rate of Rs 100 crore over the next 10-12 months. The company had earlier secured a Rs 2.5 crore investment on Shark Tank India at a Rs 50 crore valuation.

Solgram raises over $1M in pre-seed funding

Gurugram-based premium grocery platform Solgram has raised over $1 million in a pre-seed funding round led by DSG Consumer Partners and Saama Capital, with participation from hospitality entrepreneur Kapil Chopra. The capital will be used to expand its temperature-controlled cold-chain infrastructure, strengthen technology capabilities and deepen sourcing relationships. Launched in Gurugram, Solgram offers fresh produce, dairy, meat, seafood, bakery products and gourmet groceries through an integrated supply chain covering sourcing, storage and last-mile delivery. The platform also offers a health-focused selection through its Mindful Mode feature. Solgram plans to expand across the National Capital Region before entering other Tier I markets. Its business model focuses on product quality, provenance and reliability rather than delivery speed alone.

Unify Foodworks raises Rs 5 Cr to expand restaurant brands

Unify Foodworks, the exclusive pan-India master franchisee of Moe's Casa Mexicana and Carvel, has raised Rs 5 crore in seed funding through compulsorily convertible debentures. The capital will support expansion of both international food brands across the National Capital Region (NCR), where they made their India debut.

The company plans to strengthen store density, consumer awareness and operational capabilities before entering additional markets. Moe's Casa Mexicana offers Mexican-inspired dishes, including burritos, bowls and tacos, while Carvel is an American ice cream brand founded in 1934. Unify Foodworks has outlined a long-term expansion roadmap of more than 100 stores across India. The company is also developing integrated supply-chain and operating systems to support its expansion.

ECOPATH raises Rs 2.25 Cr to scale zero-cement construction tech

Bengaluru-based climate-tech startup ECOPATH has raised Rs 2.25 crore in seed funding from Social Alpha and Gemcorp to scale its zero-cement construction technology. The company has built an order book exceeding Rs 40 crore within two years of operations.

Founded by Sourabh Kumar and Abhishek Chhazed, ECOPATH develops cement-free concrete using industrial by-products, including steel-industry waste, and proprietary binders. The funding will support manufacturing capacity expansion, supply-chain development, research and team building. The company has secured over 40 commercial customers, including Lodha, Tata Power and Jindal Steel. ECOPATH says its materials can reduce carbon emissions by approximately 75% compared with conventional cement-based alternatives, depending on application and project specifications.

Mahesh Babu invests in gaming studio Shortgun Games

Actor Mahesh Babu has joined Mumbai-based gaming development studio Shortgun Games as a strategic investor to support the development of premium PC and console games. The partnership will focus on creating original intellectual properties for international markets, including North America and Europe.

The studio's flagship project, PROJECT TAKEDOWN, is a high-budget, narrative-driven action-adventure game being developed for platforms such as PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

Founded by Jeet Chandan and Vidhit Mehta, Shortgun Games is focusing on building cinematic gaming experiences from India for global audiences. The company has also brought on action director Vicky Arora to lead the game's combat design, incorporating motion-capture choreography and physical stunt mechanics.

Cellegant Energy Systems raises Rs 2.61 Cr for hydrogen-powered drones

IIT Gandhinagar professor-founded startup Cellegant Energy Systems has raised Rs 2.61 crore from investors, including GVFL Prarambh Fund Trust, CoCreate Aarambh and IIEC, IIT Gandhinagar's incubator. The funding will support the development of indigenous hybrid hydrogen fuel-cell electric drivetrain systems designed to extend the endurance of drones and unmanned aerial vehicles.

Founded by Dr Atul Bhargav, the startup's immediate priority is to demonstrate a 35-kg hydrogen-powered drone. It aims to advance the programme from technology readiness level three to six over the next six to 12 months. Cellegant is also developing energy solutions for autonomous robots, marine vehicles and other applications. The investment will support technology development, intellectual property protection and team expansion.

DBS Foundation awards Rs 7.4 Cr to India's Khyaal

DBS Foundation has awarded SGD 3 million, approximately Rs 22 crore, to four purpose-driven businesses across Asia under its Impact Beyond Award programme. India's Taisho Ventures, which operates senior citizens' platform Khyaal, will receive SGD 1 million, equivalent to approximately Rs 7.4 crore. Khyaal has more than five million users and provides services spanning physical, emotional, cognitive, social, financial and digital well-being for people aged 50 and above. The funding will help strengthen its platform and expand services into Tier II and III cities, besides exploring opportunities in Southeast Asia. The other award recipients are Hon Yang Healthcare in Taiwan, One Bite Design Studio in Hong Kong and Shanghai Fuyuan Elderly Care Service in China.

OBSESS raises angel funding to build fitness technology platform

Delhi NCR-based fitness and sports technology startup OBSESS has raised angel funding to develop an integrated digital ecosystem for India's fitness and wellness industry. The round saw participation from investors including Pushpendra Singh, Co-founder of Centricity, Amitt Goel and Harshit Vij, Co-founder of Freecultr.

Founded in 2026 by Tushar Sharma and Yash Kumar, the company is developing a platform covering gym discovery, memberships, personal training, sports venue bookings, fitness products, nutrition and wellness services. The funding amount was not disclosed. The capital will support technology development, expansion of its network of gyms and trainers, user acquisition and partnerships. OBSESS also plans to introduce AI-powered capabilities for workout planning, nutrition recommendations and personalisation.

Other news

Adobe launches programme offering free tools to eligible startups

Adobe has launched Adobe for Startups, a programme designed to help early-stage companies strengthen their branding, content creation and customer engagement capabilities. Eligible startups will receive 12 months of free access to Adobe Firefly Pro Plus, Acrobat Studio, Adobe Express Premium and Semrush.

The programme is open to startups founded within the last five years that have raised less than $15 million in funding, subject to eligibility and country availability. The offering combines AI-powered creative tools, document productivity solutions and marketing intelligence capabilities. Adobe will also provide opportunities for founders to participate in workshops, events and learning programmes with its experts. The initiative aims to help startups build their brands and scale marketing activities with limited resources.

Smarten Power Systems reports 77.4% revenue growth in H1 FY27

Smarten Power Systems has reported a 77.4% year-on-year increase in consolidated revenue from operations to Rs 204.54 crore during the first half of FY27, compared with Rs 115.26 crore in the corresponding period last year. Consolidated profit after tax more than doubled to Rs 11.99 crore, registering growth of 103.8% against Rs 5.88 crore in H1 FY26. Profit before tax increased 111.9% to Rs 15.83 crore, while earnings per share stood at Rs 6.31. On a standalone basis, revenue grew 87% to Rs 201.37 crore.

The company manufactures power backup and solar energy products, including home UPS systems, solar inverters, batteries and solar panels, with operations across 23 states and two Union Territories.

Indian enterprises lose $3M per major IT outage: New Relic

Indian enterprises are losing an average of $3 million for every high-impact IT outage, according to New Relic's 2026 Observability Forecast: India Edition. The report, based on a survey of 500 Indian respondents, found that 61% of organisations experience major outages weekly or more frequently. Nearly 31% encounter such disruptions multiple times a day.

The study also found that 56% of Indian organisations monitor AI agents in production, compared with the global average of 35%. However, developers spend nearly half their time addressing system disruptions. India also leads in OpenTelemetry standardisation, with 42% of respondents fully standardised. New Relic said fragmented monitoring tools continue to limit the benefits of advanced observability investments.

365squared launches AI-powered voice fraud protection platform

365squared, a Route Mobile company within Proximus Global, has launched 365callguard, an AI-powered voice fraud protection solution for mobile and fixed-line operators. The platform is designed to identify and prevent fraudulent calls before they reach subscribers. It addresses seven categories of fraud, including vishing, caller ID spoofing, Wangiri, international revenue share fraud, SIM box fraud, flash calls, and robocalls.

The solution combines AI models with rule-based detection to provide real-time analysis and enable automatic actions such as call blocking, caller ID modification and subscriber alerts. The launch expands 365squared's existing communications security portfolio, which includes its AI-powered messaging protection platform, 365smsguard.

FirstClub enters beauty and personal care category

FirstClub, the quality-focused consumer platform, has expanded into the beauty and personal care category under its 'Filtered for Good' initiative. The launch brings together more than 80 brands across skincare, haircare, body care and personal care, with products priced between Rs 300 and Rs 3,500.

The company has introduced an ingredient-first evaluation framework covering shampoos, cleansers, moisturisers and sunscreens. It has excluded more than 100 ingredients from its beauty selection and requires listed products to have customer ratings of at least four stars. The platform will also offer 100% ingredient disclosure on product pages and a Samples Selector feature. The expansion follows its earlier entry into grocery, pet care and home and kitchen products.

BIT Mesra and IIT Kanpur sign five-year research collaboration MoU

Birla Institute of Technology, Mesra, and IIT Kanpur have signed a five-year memorandum of understanding to strengthen academic engagement and joint research. The agreement provides for student and faculty exchanges, joint supervision of research scholars, access to specialised facilities and collaborative academic programmes. It also establishes a framework for jointly submitting research proposals to national and international funding agencies.

The MoU covers undergraduate and postgraduate research, internships, joint Master's and PhD supervision, academic programmes and staff training. Students from both institutions will be able to participate in joint research projects and access specialised laboratories. The partnership is aimed at strengthening research capabilities, technology development and academic cooperation between the institutions.

Straive partners with Anthropic for responsible enterprise AI deployment

Global data and AI company Straive has partnered with Anthropic to help enterprises build and deploy AI solutions across business workflows. The collaboration will focus on responsible AI adoption, combining Anthropic's approach to safe AI with Straive's expertise in data readiness, domain knowledge, governance and operational delivery.

The partnership aims to help organisations integrate AI into industry-specific workflows while maintaining human oversight and appropriate operational controls. Straive's Build AI and Run AI capabilities cover solution design, deployment and continuous improvement. The companies will work with enterprises to identify where AI can support business processes and where human intervention remains necessary. Straive serves sectors including financial services, healthcare, manufacturing, media, education and publishing.

Vartis Platforms launches UdhaarSaathi loan marketplace for small merchants

Vartis Platforms, the parent company of LenDenClub and InstaMoney, has launched UdhaarSaathi, a digital loan marketplace targeting UPI QR-enabled micro and small businesses. The platform aims to facilitate Rs 1,000 crore in loan disbursements by the end of the current financial year. It offers collateral-free business loans ranging from Rs 15,000 to Rs 2.5 lakh, with an average ticket size of approximately Rs 1 lakh.

Target customers include kirana stores, pharmacies, street vendors and small retailers. The platform uses banking and payment transaction data shared with merchants' consent to facilitate credit assessment by lending partners. Operating as a loan service provider, UdhaarSaathi works with multiple NBFCs and offers daily repayment structures aligned with merchants' cash flows.

TEXMiN partners Magnora to strengthen India's rare earth magnet ecosystem

TEXMiN, the Technology Translation Research Park established by the Department of Science and Technology at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad, has entered into a strategic alliance with Magnora RE Tech to explore opportunities in critical minerals, rare earth elements and rare earth permanent magnets. ELITech Earth Science will provide project management consultancy and technical coordination support.

The collaboration aims to strengthen India's domestic value chain for rare earth permanent magnets, which are essential for electric vehicles, renewable energy systems and advanced electronics. The partnership will combine research expertise, industry investment and project execution capabilities. The initiative is aligned with the National Critical Mineral Mission, Atmanirbhar Bharat and Viksit Bharat 2047, with the objective of reducing import dependence.

AMU Leasing sees 65% of EV financing disbursements from non-metro markets

AMU Leasing, an RBI-registered NBFC focused on green mobility and electric vehicle financing, has reported that 65% of its disbursements come from non-metro markets. The company has acquired approximately 14,000 customers and is strengthening its presence across 10 states. Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, West Bengal, Jharkhand and Haryana are among its fastest-growing markets. Commercial electric vehicles account for the entire financing portfolio in these markets, reflecting the company's focus on last-mile connectivity and goods transportation.

AMU Leasing is also working to establish operations in Rajasthan and Chhattisgarh. The company offers financing across electric two-wheelers, three-wheelers, four-wheelers and commercial vehicles, targeting underserved rural and semi-urban markets.

E2E Networks launches Blaze pay-per-token AI inference service

E2E Networks has launched Blaze, a pay-per-token inference service for open AI models, targeting developers and enterprises. The platform provides a single OpenAI-compatible endpoint to access multiple open models, with customers paying according to their token consumption.

Powered by NVIDIA GPU infrastructure and components from NVIDIA DSX OS, Blaze is designed for applications such as voice, coding agents, document AI, OCR and image and video generation. The service is hosted on E2E's India-based cloud infrastructure, addressing demand for data sovereignty and cost-efficient AI deployment. E2E is also expanding its AI infrastructure capacity to approximately 14.6 MW, including a 1,024-GPU NVIDIA Blackwell cluster that has been operational since May 2026.

Azim Premji Foundation launches Social Startups Programme

Azim Premji Foundation has launched a Social Startups Programme to support development sector professionals in establishing and leading civil society organisations focused on underserved communities. The first cohort will include approximately 100 participants across Odisha, Northeast India, Eastern Uttar Pradesh and Bengaluru Urban.

The programme will support areas such as rural livelihoods, healthcare, mental health, disability, children's welfare and community sanitation. Applicants must be below 40 years of age, hold a graduate degree and have at least three years of grassroots development experience. Selected participants will receive financial assistance and guidance during an eight-month seeding phase, followed by an opportunity to apply for a two-year seed grant. Applications are open from November 1 to December 31, 2026.

mFilterIt removes over 2 lakh fraudulent digital assets during festive season

Digital trust and ad-fraud intelligence platform mFilterIt has removed more than two lakh fraudulent digital assets targeting a leading Indian bank during the festive shopping season. Its monitoring uncovered 2.4 lakh fraudulent cases across 10 digital platforms, including fake websites, phishing pages, impersonation accounts and bogus promotional offers.

The company reported a takedown success rate of over 97%, with 80-85% of identified scam assets removed within 24 hours of detection. The cases included brand impersonation, coupon abuse and deceptive referral schemes. According to mFilterIt, the findings highlight the growing scale of digital fraud during high-traffic shopping periods. The company advocates continuous monitoring and digital crawling to identify and remove fraudulent infrastructure before consumers are affected.

Airtel and District rename Bengaluru concert venue Airtel Arena

Bharti Airtel and District have announced a collaboration to enhance digital connectivity at a major live entertainment venue in Bengaluru, which will be renamed Airtel Arena. The 16-acre open-air venue will receive dedicated digital infrastructure investment from Airtel to improve connectivity for fans, artists and event organisers. The venue can accommodate more than 17,000 people and has hosted performances by artists including Arijit Singh, Anirudh Ravichander and Bryan Adams.

The partnership will support high-speed connectivity, digital payments, livestreaming and other services during large-scale events. District will continue managing the consumer-facing entertainment experience, while Airtel will strengthen the venue's technological infrastructure. The initiative reflects growing investment in India's live entertainment ecosystem.

Medi Assist reports 60.2% growth in H1 FY27 net profit

Medi Assist Healthcare Services has reported a 13% year-on-year increase in operating revenue to Rs 478 crore in H1 FY27. Operating EBITDA grew 19% to Rs 97.2 crore, while profit after tax increased 60.2% year-on-year. Profit before tax rose 47% and total premiums under management reached Rs 24,752 crore. The company's group health benefits market share stood at 34.1%, with client retention of 90.5%. Technology monetisation also improved, with SaaS and licensing revenue growing 83.8% to Rs 18.1 crore during the first half.

The company's board has approved a share buyback of up to Rs 49.3 crore, funded through internal cash flows. Medi Assist said the buyback would support shareholder returns while preserving funds for expansion and technology investments.

Decentro launches Soundbox range for UPI merchant payments

Fintech infrastructure platform Decentro has launched a range of Soundbox devices aimed at small merchants and businesses accepting digital payments. The offering includes a Static QR Soundbox and a Dynamic QR Soundbox featuring a display, keypad and NFC capabilities. The devices provide audio payment confirmations and are designed to support merchants in Tier II and smaller markets, which account for approximately 45% of UPI transaction volumes.

The Static QR device supports 4G connectivity, with 2G and optional Wi-Fi backup, while payment alerts are available in multiple languages. The company is targeting one million devices by the end of 2028 and is in discussions with five partners for large-scale deployments. Decentro currently has over 5,000 offline UPI QR deployments.

Porter appoints Gaurav Jain as CFO, elevates technology and marketing leaders

Digital goods transport platform Porter has strengthened its leadership team with the appointment of Gaurav Jain as chief financial officer. The company has also elevated Shubham Gupta as chief technology officer and Mohit Rathi as chief marketing officer.

Jain joins Porter from Amazon, where he spent more than a decade, and brings over 20 years of experience in finance and strategy across e-commerce, financial services and FMCG. Gupta, who joined Porter in 2015, has led engineering and technology initiatives, including infrastructure modernisation, security and AI adoption. Rathi has been with the company for over a decade and has handled expansion and customer growth initiatives. The leadership changes come as Porter prepares for its next phase of expansion.

MathCo appoints former Unilever executive Vijay Raj to advisory board

Enterprise AI and analytics company MathCo has appointed Vijay Raj to its advisory board as it enters its second decade of operations. Raj brings three decades of experience in the insights industry, including 26 years at Unilever, where he worked on consumer behaviour and business strategy. In his new role, he will advise the company's leadership on market opportunities, customer priorities and long-term growth strategy.

His experience is expected to support MathCo's expansion in the consumer packaged goods sector and strengthen its engagement with enterprise clients.

Fulcrum Digital appoints Latha Nathan as SVP of India delivery operations

Enterprise AI and digital transformation company Fulcrum Digital has appointed Latha Nathan as Senior Vice President of India Delivery Operations. She will oversee the company's delivery organisation across its centres in Pune, Coimbatore and Mumbai. Her responsibilities will include delivery excellence, talent development, client success and scaling India operations.

Nathan joins Fulcrum Digital from Fidelity Investments, where she served as Vice President and led a business unit focused on digitisation and customer-facing platform products.

AstraZeneca appoints Naveen Krishna Yamarthi to lead Chennai innovation centre

AstraZeneca has appointed Naveen Krishna Yamarthi as managing director of AZIPL and the head of its Global Innovation & Technology Centre in Chennai, effective October 30, 2026. In his new role, he will lead the centre's development as a strategic, multifunctional innovation hub, supporting the company's global operations and Bold Ambition 2030 strategy.

Yamarthi brings more than 22 years of experience in building and scaling global capability centres (GCCs), with expertise in technology and business transformation.

UiPath appoints Yashdeep Vaishnav as India country manager

Business orchestration and automation company UiPath has appointed Yashdeep Vaishnav as managing director and country manager for India. He will lead the company's business operations, drive adoption of its automation solutions and expand its customer and partner ecosystem in the country. He has previously held senior positions at Snowflake, Salesforce, VTEX, Melento and Oracle.

AscentHR recognised as leader in NelsonHall Payroll Services 2026 assessment

HR technology and payroll services provider AscentHR has been recognised as a Leader in NelsonHall's Payroll Services 2026 – Overall assessment. The company was also named an Innovator in the Multi-Country Payroll Capability category.

The evaluation was conducted through NelsonHall's Vendor Evaluation & Assessment Tool, which assesses payroll providers on market presence, client value and technological innovation. NelsonHall cited AscentHR's payroll expertise, broad service portfolio and technology capabilities, including intelligent anomaly detection, Tia 2.0 and Smart Rules.

GoKwik announces Rs 7.57 cr ESOP liquidity programme for employees

Bengaluru-based commerce enablement platform GoKwik has announced an employee stock option liquidity programme involving a combined payout of Rs 7.57 crore to 69 employees. The participating employees are expected to realise an average return of approximately nine times their original grant value among the earliest ESOP holders.

The programme comes as the company turned adjusted EBITDA positive in October 2026, based on unaudited management accounts.

1Crowd partially exits Mojro investment, retains 75% stake

Early-stage investment firm 1Crowd has partially exited its investment in logistics technology company Mojro, generating returns of several times its original investment. The firm has sold 25% of its holding while retaining the remaining 75%, signalling its continued commitment to the company.

1Crowd first invested in Mojro in February 2018 and has supported it through three subsequent funding rounds. The partial exit took place as part of Mojro’s Series A financing, in which 1Crowd also participated alongside other investors. Mojro provides an AI-native B2B SaaS platform that helps enterprises automate logistics planning, route optimisation, scheduling and delivery operations. The platform is designed to improve efficiency, reduce logistics costs and provide visibility across goods movement.

Mobavenue reports 72% growth in H1 FY27 profit

Mobavenue AI Tech reported a 72.2% year-on-year increase in profit after tax to Rs 22.9 crore for the first half of FY27, while revenue rose 48.6% to Rs 149.6 crore. EBITDA grew 59.6% to Rs 31.6 crore, with the margin expanding 140 basis points to 21.1%. For the second quarter ended September 30, 2026, revenue increased 41.3% to Rs 76.7 crore and EBITDA rose 47.3% to Rs 16.2 crore. Profit after tax was up 54.8% at Rs 11.3 crore. Growth was driven by demand from advertisers in quick commerce, BFSI, fintech, entertainment, travel and commerce. International markets contributed 23.8% of Q2 revenue, while direct clients accounted for 64.7%. India contributed 77.7% of first-half revenue.

Avanade report highlights gap in Indian enterprises’ AI transformation

Indian businesses report high confidence in their use of artificial intelligence, but many have yet to fundamentally transform operations around the technology, according to an Avanade survey. The company’s AI Reality Report found that 82% of Indian business leaders are confident in their teams’ AI use, while only 23% said their organisations had reshaped how they work. The survey found that 44% of Indian respondents reported significant improvements in operational efficiency and 42% cited gains in employee productivity. However, 75% said AI had yet to deliver returns that justified the investment, while 74% had not formally calculated its return on investment. Integration and scaling remain challenges, with 47% reporting deployment problems. Avanade said enterprises must strengthen foundations and measure financial outcomes.

Taghash launches AI assistant for investment funds

Investment fund technology platform Taghash has launched Taghash Brain, an artificial intelligence assistant designed to streamline portfolio monitoring, reporting and daily operations for venture capital firms and other investment funds. Integrated into Taghash’s fund management platform, Brain enables investment teams to analyse fund data, generate reports, build live dashboards and execute tasks through a conversational interface. It uses information already maintained within the platform, including portfolio data, deal records and operational workflows. Taghash plans to introduce further agentic AI capabilities in the coming months.

Deel launches workforce security solution to detect hiring fraud

Global HR and payroll platform Deel has launched Deel Security, a workforce security solution designed to detect identity fraud during recruitment and throughout employment. The platform analyses risk signals across resumes, digital footprints, interviews and identity documents to identify deepfakes, proxy interviewers and suspicious identities. The launch follows rising concerns about fraudulent remote job applications. Deel research involving 1,011 HR professionals in the UK and US found that 66% of organisations had seen an increase in suspicious or potentially fraudulent remote worker applications over the past year. Some 93% of HR leaders expressed concern about deepfake or AI-generated workers.

Zelio E-Mobility begins production at new Hisar facility

Zelio E-Mobility has commenced commercial production at its new manufacturing facility in Patan, Hisar, Haryana, adding annual capacity of 48,000 electric two-wheelers and 24,000 three-wheelers. The expansion takes the company’s total installed capacity from 2.4 lakh to approximately 3.12 lakh units. Spread across six acres, the facility has a built-up area of 2.61 lakh square feet and represents an investment of more than Rs 20 crore. Production has begun for Zelio electric scooters and Tanga electric three-wheelers. The additional capacity is expected to come on stream during the third quarter of FY27. Zelio currently operates four plants and has more than 400 dealers across over 25 states.

IKF Finance targets Rs 25,000 crore AUM by 2030

IKF Finance is targeting assets under management of Rs 25,000 crore by 2030, supported by technology investments, product diversification and expansion beyond its traditional southern markets. The lender ended FY26 with consolidated AUM of more than Rs 8,600 crore, up around 30%, and reported profit after tax of Rs 215 crore. The company has expanded to more than 350 branches across 13 states and operates in vehicle, construction equipment and MSME finance. Its housing finance subsidiary offers affordable home loans. Vehicle finance now accounts for less than 70% of the group’s assets.

item.title: Ambani tops Forbes' global billionaire gainers list with $7B wealth jump as Reliance shares soar
item.description: The gains pushed Ambani to No.23 spot on the world billionaire list, making him the richest Indian ahead of Gautam Adani, who was ranked at No.26.
item.content:encoded:
Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani has emerged as the world's biggest billionaire wealth gainer, adding over $6 billion to his fortune in a single day, as shares of his flagship company surged following a stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings performance.

According to Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires list, Ambani's wealth increased by 7.85%, or $6.3 billion, making him the biggest gainer globally in the latest update to the ranking on November 2.

The gain was substantially ahead of the second-biggest wealth accretion on the list, with Spanish retail billionaire Amancio Ortega adding $1.7 billion, followed by China's Zhong Shanshan at $1.5 billion.

The gains pushed Ambani to No.23 spot on the world billionaire list, making him the richest Indian ahead of Gautam Adani, who was ranked at No.26 with a wealth of $79.12 billion, according to the Forbes listing. Ambani had a wealth of $88.8 billion, according to Forbes.

The sharp increase in Ambani's wealth coincided with a rally in Reliance Industries shares, which jumped 11.6% on Monday, marking their strongest trading session in more than six years. The stock closed at its day's high and was the biggest gainer on the benchmark Nifty 50 index.

The rally followed Reliance's September-quarter results, which showed a 40.6% year-on-year increase in consolidated net profit to Rs 25,548 crore, significantly ahead of analyst expectations. Stronger refining and petrochemical margins, alongside improved profitability at its telecom business Jio, helped drive the earnings growth.

The results reinforced investor confidence in Reliance's two major earnings engines - its oil-to-chemicals business and digital services - even as profitability in its retail business remained under pressure.

The company's refining core earnings surged 68%, while Jio Platforms' core earnings rose 16.6% during the quarter.

"Mukesh Ambani chairs and runs $125 billion (revenue) Reliance Industries, which has interests in petrochemicals, oil and gas, telecom, retail, media and financial services," Forbes said.

Reliance was founded by his late father Dhirubhai Ambani, a yarn trader, in 1966 as a small textile manufacturer. After his father's death in 2002, Ambani and his younger sibling, Anil, divided the family empire.
